title: Resonant spin mode from retarded relaxation
abstract: In ultrafast spin dynamics additional modes in the THz range appear which cannot be captured by conventional Landau-Lifshitz equations. Extending these equations by further time derivatives (inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation) solves the issue only partly. Here we suggest to explain these modes by retarded Lindbladian relaxation. In spite of the simplicity of this phenomenological approach the agreement with the experimental data is promising: physically plausible parameters describe the position and the large width of these resonances. The salient feature of several almost equidistant resonance peaks is in-line with experimental evidence as well.
summary: This work addresses the discrepancy between standard spin dynamics models and experimental observations of high-frequency spin resonances. By proposing and analyzing the retarded Lindbladian relaxation model, the authors provide a theoretically robust framework that accurately predicts the characteristic multiple resonance peaks seen in ferromagnetic materials. This advances the understanding of non-Markovian effects in ultrafast magnetism.
main_problem: The paper aims to explain additional, high-frequency spin resonance modes observed during ultrafast spin dynamics that cannot be accounted for by standard Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations.
main_result: The retarded Lindbladian relaxation model (rLLL equation) successfully predicts the existence of these multiple, equidistant resonance peaks, showing superior agreement with experimental data compared to the inertial LLG approach.
method: The authors derive and analyze the retarded LLL equation by incorporating time retardation into the quantum Lindblad framework, linearizing the resulting differential equations to compute the dynamic susceptibility.
model_or_system: The study focuses on spin dynamics in thin ferromagnetic films, such as epitaxial permalloy and cobalt, modeled using extensions of the LLG equation, specifically the retarded LLL equation.
key_observables: Resonant spin modes in the THz range, the width and frequency of these resonance peaks, and the presence of multiple, equidistant resonance peaks.
important_parameters: Damping parameter ($\lambda$), relaxation rate ($\gamma$), and the retardation time ($	au$ or $	au_i$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the observed dynamics are governed by retarded Lindbladian relaxation, which avoids the limitations of Taylor expansions inherent in the inertial LLG approach.
figures_summary: Figures compare the dynamic susceptibility data fitted by the iLLG model versus the retarded LLL model for permalloy and CoFeB films, highlighting the successful fit of the rLLL model to multiple resonance peaks.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the failure of conventional LLG/iLLG models, proposing the retarded LLL approach based on Lindblad theory, and then validating this model by comparing its predictions for resonance frequencies and peak structures against multiple sets of experimental magnetic susceptibility data.
why_interesting: The incorporation of retarded relaxation mechanisms into magnetization dynamics provides a powerful, non-Markovian extension to standard spin models, which is crucial for accurately describing ultrafast phenomena in spintronics and magnonics.

Fig. 2 First solution x of Eq. (11) as function of the parameter α. The real part defines the oscillabory circular frequency Re(x)/τ while the negative imaginary part determines the decay rate −Im(x)/τ. The relative width of the resonances decreases for increasing α.

Fig. 3 The absolute value of the susceptibility (12) is depicted. The resonances are clearly visible as peaks, at least for not too small values of α. The intrinsic width of these peaks results from the one-parameter form of the susceptibility. Strikingly, there occur many additional resonances after the first one which, however, become increasingly broader.

Fig. 4 Fit to the measured susceptibility data from Unikandanunni et al. [33]. The data was taken from a thin cobalt film of fcc structure. The theory is fitted to the first peak at finite frequency, the subsequent peaks are not fitted. In both data sets the response at low frequencies is deducted to highlight the high-frequency response.
